title: Straight into the desert (Mark 1:9–13)
hookLine: baptism, the voice, then the Spirit drives him out among the wild beasts

cards: Some storytellers linger. They give you the weather, the smell of the kitchen, what everyone was wearing. Not Mark.
Mark is the friend who tells a story so fast you have to say, wait, back up.
In five verses today, Jesus arrives from a small village, is baptized in a river, sees the sky rip open, hears a voice, and is driven out into the wilderness for forty days.
Mark has a favorite word for this speed, and you're going to start hearing it everywhere.

teach.b: First, the river. Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptizes him in the Jordan. Mark doesn't stop to explain why.
He just moves. Second, the word. In the Douay-Rheims: "And forthwith coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit as a dove descending, and remaining on him."
Older English Bibles say straightway. In Greek it's euthys, immediately, right then. Mark reaches for it again and again, and it gives his whole gospel the feeling of running.
Where the English says opened, Mark's Greek actually says the heavens were torn, ripped like cloth. And a voice from heaven says: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased.

Catholics see the whole Trinity in this moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. Fourth, the desert. Then, immediately again: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert."
Drove is a strong word, the same word Mark later uses for driving out demons. Jesus is there forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serve him. Mark gives it one sentence.
He doesn't tell us what the temptations were; Matthew and Luke do that. Mark leaves them untold, and adds a detail of his own: the wild beasts.
Beloved, and straight into the wilderness: in Mark, being loved by God doesn't mean an easy road.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT DROVE HIM OUT INTO THE DESERT.
teach.b: It means the road starts right away.

how: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that closes the Christmas season, and hear Mark's short account of the forty days in the desert on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: like a dove, then drove him out

s: Mark describes the three temptations in detail
Mark gives one sentence. Matthew and Luke tell the temptations.
Mark uses the word immediately again and again
euthys: forthwith, straightway, immediately. it gives his gospel its running pace.
Mark's Greek says the heavens were torn
the English says opened; the Greek says ripped, like cloth.

games.q: you've just been baptized, the sky has torn open, and a voice has called you beloved. what happens next in Mark?
o: the Spirit drives you straight into the desert.
games.why: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert." forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serving him.

practice: Replay your morning quickly: woke up, and straightway, phone; straightway, coffee; straightway, the next thing; and notice how few pauses there were. Now, for these two minutes, don't go straightway anywhere; stay put.
If you pray, rest in the word spoken over Jesus at the river, beloved; if you don't, just rest.

wordCard.voice: Euthys. Mark's favorite Greek word, straightway, immediately, carrying Jesus from the river to the wilderness in a single breath, his baptism and his forty days. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: straightway, immediately, Mark's favorite word.

carryVoice: Your line: straightway. Mark's favorite word, and he won't slow down. Day one hundred ninety-three.
